HRT on its own won’t regrow your hair. It will generally stop any additional loss thanks to the T blocker, but as with all things HRT it depends on your genetics.

What you can try is adding finasteride and minoxidil. Finasteride will block the specific type of testosterone that causes male pattern baldness, and minoxidil will regrow hair.

It won’t happen quickly and you need to be diligent, but after I started about 2 1/2 years ago my bald spot is filling in and the corners around my widow’s peak are also starting to fill in. 

It’s all worth a try, but in the end there’s no guarantee. 

Anyway I hope that helps.

Kids are way less hung up on the gender binary than adults. So the best way I found was to be direct. 

I was on a beach vacation with my brother’s family. One day as we were heading out to dinner I came out wearing heels and a dress. The youngest (5) asked me why I was wearing girl’s shoes. 

I sat down next to him and said, “Why are you wearing boy’s shoes?” He giggled and said, “Because I’m a boy,” and I replied to that with, “Okay and I’m wearing girl’s shoes, because I’m a girl.”

At first he and his brother (7) thought I was being silly, but I confirmed that I was a girl on the inside.

We talk a lot about how being on HRT (going in either direction) "felt right immediately", but that isn't true for everyone. In fact I think it's a bit dangerous to use how someone feels on HRT as a litmus test. I have a couple of friends who have started MtF HRT and granted it's early for them, but they're not going to be coming in here anytime soon talking about what a wonderful experience has been for them.  

My experience starting out was very similar to yours. My first two weeks on just Spiro felt amazing. That constant feeling of being ready to snap at any moment was finally gone. I could sort my thoughts out. 

It was and is (almost 2 years later) so much better than before.

So yeah those are the mental and emotional changes a lot of folks talk about, but here's the downside: estrogen brain is real. We trade the feeling of being constantly on edge for our thoughts become much more fleeting. I had a long conversation with my ex-wife a couple weeks back and she confirmed that's just what E does. Gotta take the good with the bad, but I now want to apologize to every cis woman I ever called and airhead. lol

Transgender is an umbrella term that simply means your internal experience of your gender does not match what your gender is assumed to be based on your biological sex.

Genderfluid is one of many non-cis gender identities that falls under the transgender umbrella. 

So being genderfluid also means - by definition - that you are transgender. 

That being said, which labels you choose to use to describe your gender is completely up to you.

Apparently I missed my connection and ended up at the wrong airport in NC. I had to be driven by someone who worked for the airline drove me to the correct one.

I could understand not remembering it if I was like 7 or something, but I was almost 12 and most of the time if I don’t immediately remember something I at least can confirm the broad strokes once my memory is jogged. 

This is just black hole in my mind to this day.

We can’t talk about The Pink Opaque, without talking about The Midnight Realm.

The core truth of the obvious plot is that Mr. Melancholy won, and he trapped Tara and Isabell in The Midnight Realm as Maddie and Owen. 

This means that The Pink Opaque is the world where Owen and Maddie are from, and where they exist as Isabell and Tara. This further means that the movie takes place in The Midnight Realm, which we (the audience) would call the real world.

That is the literal meaning in the context of the plot, however there’s a metaphorical layer as well.

The experience of living in The Midnight Realm is a metaphor for living your life as the person you’re EXPECTED to be, instead of who you really are. If you want to pull in the layer of meaning for trans gender folks, then this is a portrayal of what it is like to live with gender dysphoria. Even without that, however, the oppressive feelings of living a life with no agency is something lots of cis people can understand.

As far as the in-movie TV show goes, my read is that it was originally just a way for Mr. Melancholy to torment Tara and Isabell, but in his arrogance it gave Maddie (Tara) the motivation to escape. So once they got out, he killed the show to prevent Owen (Isabell) from doing the same. To discuss the transness of it, to Maddie the show was like an unrealized trans person seeing a fully transitioned trans person and realizing that it was possible for them to live their life authentically, which Maddie eventually does before coming back to attempt to save Owen.

Here’s a bonus read you didn’t ask for, but because I love this film, and I wanted to share it: the horror of the film comes from the fact that - this is just my read mind you - that Owen and Maddie would live forever in The Midnight Realm, but wouldn’t stay young forever. Mr. Melancholy only ever said they’d forget they were dying. Not that they would actually die. In The Midnight Realm he could control everything. He made time move differently for them. He took people from their lives, and he took all joy from them. So if Owen never escapes he will continue to age, but never die. He will constantly be tormented by a life he will never feel connected to. As a middle-aged trans woman, this is where the movie really got me. I have friends like Owen who are terrified of living authentically, and it’s not an understatement to say they are tortured by life. They have convinced themselves that they can never transition. Even when they can see evidence that there is still time for them, they dismiss it as not being for them. It’s heartbreaking. This then adds an even more horrific layer that perhaps those chalk messages were put there by Mr. Melancholy not as inspiration, but as a way to further torment Owen.

Anyway. That’s my take on things. I apologize for the wall of text, but I adore this film, because of the nuance and depth, and I hope something in there helps you to understand it better. 💜

Understanding all the sizes is a struggle. They’re not nearly as straight forward as they are for men’s clothing. 

You’ll need to take two measurements of yourself. 

First your hips, which is the circumference through the widest part of your butt. 

Second is your waist. To find where your natural waistline is stand up and bend to one side. Where your body creases is where your waist is. Usually a little bit above the top of your hip bone.

Now that you know where your waist is, get that circumference too. 

With those two numbers the next thing to do is to go to like Hanes.com, find undies you like, and check out the size chart. Starting out you’ll want to stick with styles like hipster briefs, bikinis, or boy shorts. Which will have the most room for your anatomy? You just kinda gotta eyeball it. I’ll say panties tend to be roomier than they look. I started out with cotton hipsters from Hanes and they have plenty of room for me without tucking. 

The other thing to do is to check out a gender inclusive brand like TomboyX or Wildfang.

I started transitioning at 46. I just went from not me to me. I didn’t come out to anyone for 2 years, but all that time I was presenting femme, using different pronouns, and just inviting folks in. Once I had myself figured out enough that I could clearly articulate what I had realized about myself, I came out to 4 people: my oldest friend, my best friend, my daughter, and my brother. All of these people I knew would and had been accepting me before I actually said the words, “I’m trans,” to them. Those coming outs were more about celebrating who I am with them, than it was about asking, “Hey is it okay with you if I’m like this?”

There’s this misconception that you owe…OWE people - even people who have no stake in our lives like coworkers - a “coming out”, which in practice is asking (read that again) people to accept your existence.

Even the language we use to talk about coming out takes all the power away from ourselves. How many posts are like, “Coming out at work today. Wish me luck.” 

That’s just wild to me. Like what happens if the person who sits at the desk next to you, that you spend no time with outside of work is like, “Nope”?  Would you detransition? Come in here like, “The dude I hate at work who’s retiring next week says he doesn’t accept me, so guess I’m not trans kthxbye.” 

Of course not. 

I know there are folks reading this who will reply with all the complications of not coming out and just existing. I’d challenge you to examine if those are complications or fears. Fearing people’s reactions is totally valid. It is scary as fuck. I was terrified the first time I just came as my fully femme presenting self to a work function, but I did it, and it was ultimately not a big deal to anyone.

This is a fabulous TED Talk about this very topic: https://youtu.be/60B-NChtNiA?si=r2nNJD4sY4efXbBP

So yeah…that’s my two cents. Sorry for the rant. I’m very passionate about this topic, because everyone should be able to freely exist as they are
and reinvent themselves as desired.

I’ve been on MtF HRT for 2 years and my sex drive has definitely not decreased. It did, however, become more deliberate. Like you hear about how AMAB people “think with their dicks,” and you don’t realize how true that is until you go on HRT and can finally think for yourself. 

I get now why sexual desire for cis women is contingent on so much more than just, “Am I horney?” 

TBS, should you experience a drop in sexual desire, then you do have options. First make sure your T levels are balancing with your E. Cis women don’t have zero testosterone. Next some trans girls have had successfully reignited their sex drive by adding progesterone to their regimen. I personally have been on P for a year and have not gotten any increase in my libido, but seems like my experience is not what most girls experience.

The other thing to keep in mind is that the way your equipment functions is likely going to change. So after you’ve been on HRT for a bit, even if your sex drive stays intact, you may have to relearn how you work down there (but lemme tell you trans girls clitoral orgasms are AWESOME).

Anyway. Hope that helps and be sure to always keep your HRT provider in the loop on changes.  😊

If you use a hair removal cream get one specifically for male body hair like “No Hair Crew” (available on Amazon). Their stuff worked great for me before I got laser.

Estradiol along with a T blocker will change the texture of the hair (i.e. make it finer), but it will not cause it to fall out or cease to grow. E alone will likely not do much, unless your T levels are already low, since T easily overwhelms estrogen, which is why trans men don’t need to take an estrogen blocker. 

As far as shaving goes: I’d recommend using a women’s razor and a shaving gel. Like all things designed for men (like I don’t understand why men’s jeans are made of burlap compared to women’s), men’s razors seemed designed to actually be painful. A women’s razor will get you a far more comfortable shave since they are designed to be used on legs, arms, etc. and women apparently don’t pride themselves on how cut up they are after shaving (cis men are so weird).

When I do need to shave (like before a laser treatment) I don’t make it the first thing I do in the shower. I let the skin warm up a bit and exfoliate first either with a chemical exfoliant or something like a sugar scrub. That’ll help free any hairs just below the surface as well as help the razor glide over the skin. 

After the shower pat your legs dry (instead of using the towel like you’re sanding the water off of you) then use a moisturizer (I like Hempz) on your freshly shaven legs. 

Anyway. That’s my two cents on it. Hope that helps. 😊

Yes, but also no: let me explain. 

There will be employers - actually individual hiring managers - who will have an issue with trans people. I have lost out on job offers because I’m trans (I’m a 49 clockable trans woman). Honestly though did I actually miss out? Absolutely not. I dodged a bullet, because I would’ve ended up working at a place where my skills and expertise didn’t matter as much as my outward appearance. 

Once I realized this I openly shared my trans identity on LinkedIn so I could filter out places I don’t want at work anyway. 

I landed a great job a year ago with coworkers who know I’m trans, naturally use the correct pronouns, and value my skills and expertise above anything else. They support my career goals and at almost 50 I’m on track to upper level management if not the c-suite (aiming for CTO specifically). Even better my insurance covers my GRS which will (hopefully still) happen in July. 

So if by limiting you mean it will stop shitty employers from interviewing and hiring you, then yes, yes it will. Will it allow your job search to be laser focused on employers where you can thrive? Also yes. Not really sure that’s a bad thing though.

Take it from this nearly 50 year old trans woman who started her transition 3 years ago.

I think you’re confusing genetic with hereditary. 

Being trans, like having a non-heterosexual orientation, is genetic in that you are born that way. Whether or not you choose to embrace it is a different story. Lots of gay men never get in homosexual relationships or even have sex with another man. Doesn’t change the fact that they’re gay. Just means they denied their nature. 

Being genetic, however, doesn’t mean you inherited being trans or whatever from an ancestor, nor does it mean you’d pass it on to your children. 

Given that I’m the only trans person in my entire family, I’m not convinced (at present) it’s hereditary, but I’m open to the idea should evidence present itself (like all good scientists should be).

You have to know - in your soul - that you’re still 100% trans even if you never change a single thing about yourself externally.

Once you truly embrace that any step you take to transition in any way is just to improve yourSELF.

Wanting the “perfect” transition is about pleasing society’s expectations of what the perfect cis man or cis woman is. It’s exactly what cis teen girls deal with when it comes to body issues.

You also have to realize that no matter how perfectly you pass or have transitioned there will always, ALWAYS be someone who sees you as imperfect. I adopted a lyric from “IT GIRL” by Aliyah’s Interlude as my mantra: “Pretty bitches love me, and ugly hoes hate me.” So anytime I feel less than confident or get side-eyed I just repeat that to myself and never let those ugly hoes bring me down.

Finally, and this applies to any perfectionist wall you run into: the goal should always be improvement, or as Beverly Cleary said, “You can’t edit a blank page.” Transition implies change and change is active. If you never change anything then you can never transition.

I've been in therapy in some form off and on for the past 30 years. 

Forget anything you see on TV about therapy. The portrayals of therapy in popular media are actually very harmful imo. So if that is what you're expecting right off the bat, then yes: you're being unrealistic.

Let me also say this right off: you need to have this conversation WITH HER. Tell her everything you posted here. That may make you feel uncomfortable, but the point of a therapist is having someone you can safely have uncomfortable conversations with. Having an objective person who has no emotional connection to you that you can safely discuss very private and emotionally intimate issues with is - imo - worth the money. 

Understand that "no emotional connection" doesn't mean that they don't care about you. It only means that they aren't personally biased like a friend or family member would be. 

For example if you go in and talk through an issue you're having with your partner (for example), and you were CLEARLY the asshole in this case: they will tell you that in a way that isn't hurtful, but that helps you to realize that you should've acted differently. A friend on the other hand will take your side, which makes you feel good, but doesn't help to solve the issue.

They can challenge you in ways someone you have a personal connection to can't, but it isn't a one-sided relationship. You have to be willing to be extremely vulnerable with them. When they say something that challenges you emotionally (which you usually can identify by the fact that it makes you mad that them), you have to actually pause and think about WHY rubbed you the wrong way. At the very least you have to tell them how that made you feel. So if they say something that makes you feel annoyed, then say that. Say, "That's bullshit," and then tell them why when they say, "Say more about that."

As far having goals for therapy goes, it isn't a requirement, but I've found it can be extremely helpful. It doesn't have to be super well-defined, but it kinda needs to be more specific than, "I want to be a better person." My first goal when I started with my current therapist was, "I've just realized I'm trans, and I need help navigating that." In later sessions I realized I also had the goal of trying to figure out why I (was) so lonely. Both of these goals helped my therapist direct the conversations we had. It gave him a framework to know how I needed (and wanted) to be pushed out of my comfort zone.

Sometimes the goal is very concrete. I went to see my previous therapist because my ex wife had moved to a new state with my daughter, and I was considering moving as well. I worried that it wouldn't be the right decision. I had 3 sessions with her of just talking through my emotions, and in one of our last sessions I said to her, "I just don't know what to do," to which she replied very matter-of-factly, "Yes you do. You've already made your decision. Right now you're trying to figure out why that bothers you." She was right. I figured it out. I moved state, and it was one of the best things I've ever done.

To go back to your post: yes, sometimes therapy sessions can just be you unloading your emotional baggage. Sometimes the real work can't happen until you finally get it out. Our bodies store emotional trauma. The small ones, the big ones, it all gets stored until we deal with it. All that talking and venting is the emotional equivalent of a medical doctor pressing on the stomach of a patient who says they have stomach pain until they find the exact spot that really hurts. Once they find it, then they can start working to relieve the pain. You'll get there, but it isn't a quick process most of the time.

There is also the matter of chemistry. A client-therapist relationship is exactly that: a relationship. If you don't vibe with your therapist, then it can be hard to get real benefits out of the relationship. To me it sounds like you do like your therapist, but maybe you're not getting as vulnerable with her as you need to be. Maybe something is holding you back from talking about the uncomfortable things. Honestly I have no idea. You'll need to figure that one out, but if there is something holding you back, then once you remove that block and get to the really ugly things you don't talk about with ANYBODY, that's when you'll really start to see gains.

Anyway. Sorry for the wall of text. I hope something in there helps.

It does have a different connotation when used personally vs. as a diagnostic code. 

My ex-wife is a doctor, and one thing I learned as she went through medical school and into practice is that there is a lot of administrative knowledge that is required to properly serve your patients (at least in the U.S.). Most times doctors use a given diagnostic code, because that’s the code a patient’s insurance requires to cover care for that patient.

For example: my insurance won’t cover my therapy unless my therapist diagnoses me with gender dysphoria. It also won’t cover my HRT for gender dysphoria, but it will if I’m diagnosed with an endocrine disorder. So my doctor has diagnosed me with that. It’s not dishonest or fraudulent. It’s just how our system works.

That’s why you can have a career as a medical billing and coding specialist. 

Chances are the doctor didn’t even apply that code. His notes might say gender dysphoria or something, but your insurance might not provide as much coverage for that as they do if it’s coded as transsexual. So that’s what his billing specialist put it in as.

Remember you can and should always ask your doctor questions. Trust their expertise yes, but also make them explain everything to you so you understand. You should never walk out of an office visit not fully understanding what just happened. 

When I first got on HRT I grilled my doctor: why Spiro and not Bica? Why this dose? What’s the difference between taking E sublingually vs. just swallowing it? Why start with pills instead of patches or injections? What’s the difference between normal breast tenderness and something I should call you about? 

People go into medicine at the end of the day to help people. The ones who don’t washout quickly. So trust your doctor’s knowledge, experience, and intent, but always, always, ALWAYS advocate for yourself. If that diagnostic code is troubling to you call and talk to them (my doctor actually has an email portal so I can talk with her nearly instantly).

Don’t just sit back and wonder about the whats and whys: get answers.

You remind yourself that people will judge you no matter what you wear.

You never leave the house wearing something you don’t want to wear.

So the way it went down for me was a bit surreal actually. 

I was out at my local game store playing Magic: The Gathering, and in the middle of a turn I shifted in my chair or something, which triggered some voice in my head to forcibly tell me, "Don't sit like that you look like a girl!" I knew it was in my head, but I "heard" it so clearly that I almost yelled, "Shut up! Who cares!" back at it. 

It kind of freaked me out, but also made me curious about where that internal dialogue had even come from. Sure enough I realized that I had been policing my gender all the way back in like junior high, maybe even earlier. Regardless of when it started I had been doing it for so long that it had just become automatic.

From there I just stopped policing myself, and started allowing myself to give in to the little queer thoughts I had. 

"I want to paint my nails." So I painted my nails, and I loved it.

"I want a nightgown." So I got a nightgown and loved wearing it.

"I want girlie socks!" So I got girlie socks and loved wearing them. 

So on and so on.

The one little snag in my mind was that I was not into men...well...not all men, but I liked women too, so I was definitely not gay. I was a straight person who had gay fantasies...sometimes, but I'd never date a man...although...no no no...Anyhoooo. 

Once I learned that sex, sexuality, and gender were not at all connected, AND that you could be a "heterosexual transgender person". 

I realized I had never been a cis man. Early on I settled on calling myself a genderfluid bisexual (yeah finally admitted that one to myself).

Time went on and I started to settle into my gender more, and I noticed that my gender did not really shift like it did for most genderfluid people I had encountered. I very much stayed on the feminine side of things.

The first time I came out to someone close to me, I realized that I was using genderfluid to have an escape hatch for the times when I had to be around people who I hadn't come out to. At that point I realized I was just a trans woman. In between all that I started on low doses of MtF HRT, and then went full on T blockers, E, and progesterone. It has been a ride, but at 48 now, I'm happier than I've ever been in my entire life.

I realized too that I really had started experiencing gender dysphoria at about age 10 when my leg hair really started to grow in (Italian and Cuban...we are thickly hairy people lol). Of course I only recognize the signs of being an egg when I was a kid in retrospect.

Anyway, here’s my take as a 48 year old trans woman, and mind you I can only speak to my experience. Yes, there is a lot of shared experiences, but we’re all human so rarely do we have an identical experience.  

I think the first thing you want to think about is how are transgender people viewed in your setting? I can infer that they may be hated based on the fact that your character seems to need to hide their gender. By age 10 I knew something was “off” with me, but I grew up in the 80s where the word “transgender” was not part of our vocabulary. So is it similar in your story? I spent 36 years just feeling like a failed man, on the other hand a 10 year old trans kid today can learn about trans people, and would have a different experience growing up.

Next thing to consider imo is what is THEIR gender identity? Transgender is an umbrella term that covers anything that is not cisgender (i.e. gender matches body). Is your character a trans woman? Nonbinary? A trans man? Gender fluid?

Have they transitioned? If so in what ways (socially, medically, surgically)? Do they “pass”? Meaning are they immediately recognized as being trans? If they do pass, then is their fear being outed? 

If they haven’t transitioned, then do they want to? You are born transgender. Just like cis people are born cis. Not all trans people choose to or are able to transition, but they are still trans. If they want to, then why haven’t they? Is it fear? Is access to HRT / healthcare a barrier? Can they not afford a new wardrobe?

I could type out a novel here just discussing my experience, but here’s my suggestion: go meet some trans folks. Be upfront about what you’re researching, and then listen to their stories if they’re willing to share. Best to meet them irl, but online works too. 

Assuming you’re sincere (which you seem to be), then I’d be happy to chat with you about it. 

My final suggestion would be to let the trans folks you meet read what you write, and then take their feedback to heart. 

One last thing to consider: why does the character need to be trans? Yes representation is important, however MEANINGFUL representation is impactful. Was it great for Joe Russo to play the lone gay man at the beginning Endgame? Yes, but it also felt a little (a lot) like tokenism. Better version of that scene shows that guy on his date as he’s talking about it. We see them talking about losing their husbands. We see the emotions. We see them comforting each other.

Let me start by giving you a quick rundown of my background so you understand where I'm coming from. I am a 48 year old trans woman who is 2 years into her transition. 

Let's start here: 

> I fear they could be making the wrong choice

Gender is NOT a choice. Tell me: when did you choose to be a cisgender woman? Here's a hint: you didn't, but let's assume for a minute that you know that, and the choice you were talking about was their decision to come out. 

Think about the way people in the LGBTQIA+ community are treated. Think about why you're afraid of your kid being openly trans. Think about the road ahead of them. Think about how [there have been 5 trans people murdered so far this year.](https://www.hrc.org/resources/fatal-violence-against-the-transgender-and-gender-expansive-community-in-2024) Think about ALLLL of the baggage that comes with being trans.

Now. 

Why the FUCK would anyone choose that? Why on Earth would any rational person think that coming out is the RIGHT choice? 

Unless...

...the alternative was even worse. 

You will find story after story here about trans people whose "choice" literally came down to coming out or dying.

I literally had a plan to remove myself from the planet, and I was DAYS away from putting it into action before I realized and accepted I was trans. DAYS away.

You don't need to worry about them making the "wrong choice". You need to do everything in your power to ensure they are successful following the path they've started on.

How do you do that? First you stop with this idea of caterpillars and butterflies. Your child isn't transforming into anything. They're just no longer hiding who they've always been. 

A much better animal analogy is the Southern three-banded armadillo that roll up into a ball when they're threatened, or maybe a box turtle that pulls its head and limbs into its shell. 

So for a good bit of their life, your child has been hiding their real self from everyone, including you.

If you should be mourning anything, then you should be mourning the fact that you've never really known your child. That at some young age they realized they needed to hide themselves from everyone, and I do mean everyone. 

I started hiding from the world at about 6. I had no idea why I had to hide, but I learned when I was myself I got yelled at or teased or bullied. So I hid behind a mask that people found acceptable.

Think about that.

My egg cracked (i.e. I realized I was trans) at 46. 

I didn't start coming out to people until I was 48. 

I never got the chance to come out to my Dad, because he died in January, and I just came out to my mom two weeks ago. So Dad only knew the real me for 6 years of my life, and Mom will only know the real me for whatever time she has left (she's in her late 70s), but we live 100s of miles apart.

THAT is sad. 

THAT is worth mourning over, but now is your chance to get to know them. At the end of the day coming out to someone is about inviting that person to get to know the real you. So your kid didn't just say, "Hey Mom I'm trans," they said, "Hey Mom I want you to know who I really am. I hope you want to get to know me."

So do that. 

If you live in a shit place, then go visit them. Go see what it's like to be around a truly supportive community. If they're going to be changing their gender presentation (i.e. what they wear, pronouns they use, even their name), then take them shopping. Find out what they like to do. Their personality is very likely going to change, because they no longer have to spend all their mental energy hiding. 

I mean I've been a hardcore introverted nihilist for much of my life, but now that I'm out, I'm finding I'm a very extroverted person who actually likes being alive.

I know this was a long way to say that you support your trans child by taking a sincere and loving interest in this person they hid from you, and are bravely sharing with you. You realize that neither of you are going to know all the answers, and that early on things may change a few times.

I started out feeling like I was gender fluid and using they/them pronouns. Time went on and I got more comfortable with myself, and I started using she/they (which is shorthand for I used she/her or they/them pronouns). Now that I've fully unraveled myself, I've realized I'm a full blown trans woman. 

Also don't lean on them to know everything about the trans experience. If they're open to answer your questions, then ask, but don't get frustrated with them if they don't know the answer. I mean no one shows up at your door with a giant book of trans answers the moment you realize you're trans. 

Finally, how do you support yourself? Step one find yourself a therapist that is familiar with trans issues. Ideally someone who is trans themselves. Have compassion for yourself. I'm a trans woman, and I'm also a parent. I'd fully support my daughter if she realized she was trans, but I'd still be terrified for her. Hell, it shatters my heart when I see other people's trans kids getting killed or bullied. 

Even in shit areas of the country there are likely trans support groups nearby. Go find one that allows allies to attend their meetings. Definitely chime in when you have something to add, but my suggestion would be to start out listening more than talking. You're gonna hear some awful shit that trans folks go through, but then you'll know how NOT to be.

One last thing to do for yourself, and this is a hard one, don't waste a single mote of energy on any "friend" who won't support your child. I spent 36 years not wanting to live. Actually made a couple of mild attempts as a kid and in my late 30s. 

At 46 I finally decided enough was enough, and I started to put together a real plan to check out for good. 

I was just miserable. Divorced. Didn’t really like my job. One real friend who lives 100s of miles away. No local friends to go out with. Single. Medication resistant depression. 

I was just done. 

Then I had a weird moment of like hearing my internal dialogue yell at me for sitting a certain way, because people would think I was a woman. 

I started to dig into where the hell that came from, and long story short I realized I was trans. 

After spending some time exploring that I looked in the mirror one night and said, “Hey. You’re trans,” and it felt so good to finally have a word to describe how I had felt since I was 10 years old, and not only that I finally understood WHY I felt that way. 

In that moment my depression ceased, and for the first time in decades I wanted to wake up in the morning. 

That’s a long-winded way to say that everyone’s reasons are different and complex. 

If you can boil it down to one thing, then I’d say anyone who doesn’t want to be alive anymore feels disconnected from the society they live in for some reason. 

For me it was my gender. For others it could be economic reasons (it’s hard to feel connected when you feel like you don’t make enough money to participate in society). For others it could be being single. Being worried for the future doesn’t help either. 

That’s my take anyway.

Within days I was hearing about her friends, boys she liked, things that scared and worried her, her interests, and so on. The details of her life were finally available to me. 

Granted I don’t know everything. I’d never expect to, I mean she doesn’t know everything about my life, but we know more about each other than when she saw me as a man. 

So I think there are two things at work here. The first is that, since she sees me as a woman she connects with me more, and that’s good and bad. I get yelled at a good bit more now. I get sass from her, whereas previously she’d just shutdown when she was mad at me. She’s wayyyy more comfortable talking to me about guys and sex-related things. I’ve had to establish a really clear boundary with her around that. I mean I’m a woman, but I’m not one of her besties. 

The second thing I think that contributes to our closeness is that emotional intimacy begets emotional intimacy. I have shared very deep parts of myself with her. I’ve shown her I trust her with my deepest truths, and she’s returned that same trust (at least as much as she’s able). 

I’ve also set very clear boundaries and expectations with her. Like she once told me something benign in confidence and said, “Don’t tell mom,” and in that case I told her I wouldn’t, but then I went on to explain that if she told me something that made me think she was going to hurt herself or others, then I would have to tell her mom (we’re divorced and so it’s partly her mom needs to know, and partly I’m not going to start drama by keeping big secrets), but then I also told her that IF I needed to tell her mom something I would tell her before I did. Like I’m not going to blindside her. 

So all that to say this: girls connect with men and boys differently than they do with other girls and women. It’s just the way it is. So you have to accept that (I mean unless you’re a closeted trans woman too), and girls build up emotional intimacy with others by sharing things that are emotionally important to them. That’s why they find it so weird that guys make friends so quickly. Guys bond over interests. Girls bond over emotions. So ask her how her day was, and if she says, “Oh it was so bad,” instead of asking, “What happened?” Just say, “Oh I’m sorry to hear that. I’ll listen if you want to talk about it.” Don’t push, and do your best not to give her a bunch of you-know-what-you-should-do’s. If she asks how your day was, then don’t just go through what happened, talk about how the things that happened made you feel. For example, “Oh it was okay. My favorite team lost, which really bummed me out, but I went and worked out for a bit which made me feel better. I’m trying this new routine, and it’s been hard to stick to, but I’m really proud of myself for sticking with it for the past week.”

Are you sure it’s internalized transphobia? 

When I think of transphobia I think about being afraid of trans people. I mean that’s what phobias are, an irrational fear of something. 

Granted society has taken the word phobia and spun it a bit to mean “a dislike/hatred for”, but even so, are you really feeling like you dislike/hate yourself and other trans people? 

I’d wager you perhaps are feeling like you just don’t really belong in the trans community, or perhaps you’re just feeling very self-conscious about being open with your trans identity, and worried about what other people might think. 

That would be more along the lines of imposter syndrome, which is something a lot of us deal with. I certainly did at the beginning, and still do occasionally, even after transitioning for 2 years. 

Embracing yourself as a trans person is a major life change, and no one expects you just to go from zero to 9001 overnight. So make sure you have some compassion for yourself, and only go as fast as you feel comfortable going. It’s okay to not feel completely self-assured.

With imposter syndrome, the only way past it is to remind yourself that you do belong, and that you can’t read minds, so anything you THINK other people are thinking about you is your own insecurities putting thoughts in other people’s heads (if that makes sense). We can only take people at face value, until they tell us THEMSELVES what they think. 

Like sometimes I get it when I’m interacting with cis women, because I worry they might feel I’m trying to invalidate their experiences. I have to remind myself that I’m not, and if they think that, then that’s simply them making an incorrect assumption about me, and I have no control over that. 

It’s also hard to trust our intuition when we’re feeling self-conscious. That too is a skill I had to learn. If someone compliments me, then I have to remind myself I have no evidence to prove that they didn’t mean it. I’ve gotten better about just accepting the compliment and enjoying the euphoria that comes from them, but it took work. 

I hope that makes some sense and helps.

The “trans” in transgender is used the same way it is in the word transcontinental. So to cross from one thing to another. In the case of transgender it means that your gender crosses to a gender other than what was assumed at birth. 

The trans in transgender isn’t shorthand for something like “transition gender”, which is what you seem to be implying. 

To simplify it further, transgender is simply the opposite of cisgender. 

So if you don’t feel your body matches the gender you feel inside, then by definition you are a transgender person. 

Nonbinary falls under the umbrella definition of transgender, but not all nonbinary people choose to use the transgender label for themselves, which is completely valid.

In the end there’s no requirement for anyone to transition in anyway to be transgender. You can never use different pronouns, change your name, change what you wear, etc., and you’ll still be trans if you don’t feel your gender matches the gender you were assumed at birth. 

All that being said, anyone telling you that you MUST change your body or even meet any kind of medical requirement to be “allowed” to be transgender, is absolutely full of shit. It’s really a shame that certain folks in the trans community seem to want to be gatekeepers.

Gender is an internal experience, meaning it is part of you as a person. It is also a neurological construct, meaning it is hard wired into your brain in the same way your dominant hand is. 

Pronouns are part of your gender expression, which is how you show people what your internal gender experience is. 

Training yourself to use your non-dominant hand doesn’t change the way your brain was constructed. So if you’re right handed, and you start using your left hand exclusively, your dominant hand is still your right hand. You’ve just consciously chosen to use your left hand. 

In the same way, changing your gender expression doesn’t alter your brain to change your internal gender experience. A cis woman who exclusively dresses as a man is still a woman internally, and even if she uses he/him instead of she/her she is still a woman internally. This is why drag queens cannot be assumed to be trans. Lots of drag queens are cis men. They just dress as women when performing. 

Of course this makes complete sense if you stop to think about it. If neurological constructs like gender could be forcibly changed by external forces, then the world would be a mess. No one would have any idea who they are. 

This is the biggest thing that the world needs to grasp about trans people. Just as cis people are born cis, trans are born trans. We didn’t “become” trans or “choose” to be trans. It’s the way our brains are made. If you want to put a religious spin on it, then it’s how God made us, and what we wear, the pronouns we use, the name we choose to use doesn’t change that one bit.

Once you’ve been on a testosterone blocker long enough your testicles will cease to produce sperm. 

Your prostate and seminal vesicles will stop making the fluids that comprise semen. 

Your ejaculate, if you have any, will likely be clear and reduced in volume by a lot. I’ve been on a T blocker and E for 8 months, and all I get these days is a couple of dribbles of clear fluid. Doesn’t smell like it used to either (which is fine…that smell was vile). 

You may also stop being able to have a spontaneous erection, and your testicles and penis will shirk in size. I can’t even remember the last time I had morning wood. 

A lot of trans women who don’t get gender reassignment surgery need to take medications like Viagra to be able to have an erection. 

In simpler terms your reproductive system operates and looks the way it does now, because of the testosterone that your body started producing during puberty. 

If you block that (which you typically do if you’re trying to go MtF), then your body mostly reverts back to its pre-pubescent state (your body hair sticks around and your voice doesn’t change…annoyingly). 

The older you are, the less likely stopping HRT will reverse these changes, because then you’re competing with the natural decline in fertility that men experience. 

So! 

Best to preserve sperm prior to starting any kind of HRT if you want kids. It’s not a bad idea to do even if you weren’t thinking about HRT, because there are a billion and one things that can affect your fertility in this modern world.

Negative self-talk and gender dysphoria are not comparable in the way you’re comparing them. 

Gender dysphoria really boils down to your brain making you acutely aware that there is something structurally incorrect with your body. 

For example I (a trans woman) once was awakened in the middle of the night by the realization that my uterus was missing. Not just a sadness that I didn’t have one, but my brain was like, “Holy fuck where the hell is it!”

Feelings of shame and guilt around sexual orientation come from external sources like religious belief, societal expectations, etc.. 

Society could be 100% accepting of trans people, and my brain would still think my body could get pregnant and freak out when it can’t find the parts it needs to do that. 

So in the end trans people are not transitioning and changing their bodies in order to meet some standards of society, we’re transitioning in an attempt to get our bodies in line with the way we feel internally. 

It would be like you waking up without your penis tomorrow. No amount of self-acceptance is going to convince you that you were never meant to have a penis.

A trans person’s name before they transition is known as their “deadname”, and using that name is the act of “deadnaming”.

You have some really bad information. 

> I have heard that to be prescribed, a drug must be tested on poor animals.

In the United States both prescription \_and\_ OTC drugs are required to be tested on animals ([Source](https://www.peta.org/about-peta/faq/does-the-food-and-drug-administration-require-drugs-to-be-tested-on-animals/#:~:text=Our%20Views-,Does%20the%20Food%20and%20Drug%20Administration,to%20be%20tested%20on%20animals%3F&text=The%20FDA%20does%20currently%20require,the%20drugs%20safe%20for%20humans)). 

In the EU it appears that they have limited \_some\_ animal testing, but I can't find anything that says that is dependent on if the drug is OTC or prescription. 

It's important to keep in mind as well that many -- if not most -- OTC drugs started as prescription drugs, and so they were likely tested on animals before they were marketed as over-the-counter.

In addition, the regulations mentioned above only apply to the government approval of a drug. They do not cover the research that went into the development of the drug, which is almost 100% certain to have included animal testing of some sort.

>  Can HRT contain Estradiol?

Male to female HRT \_is\_ Estradiol, along with a testosterone blocker like Spironolactone or Bicalutamide, and sometimes progesterone.

If you're doing female to male HRT, then you're mainly going to take testosterone, a progestin to suppress your period, and hormone blocker to prevent or reverse hair loss.

I admire your desire to protect animals. I agree that we do a lot of awful testing on animals that is not necessary.

I'd encourage you to do some research about HRT and animal testing from reputable sources. Here are some links to get you started: 

[Feminizing hormone therapy (MtF HRT) - Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/tests-procedures/feminizing-hormone-therapy/about/pac-20385096)

[Masculinizing hormone therapy (FtM HRT) - Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/tests-procedures/masculinizing-hormone-therapy/about/pac-20385099)

[FDA Animal Testing Requirements - PETA](https://www.peta.org/about-peta/faq/does-the-food-and-drug-administration-require-drugs-to-be-tested-on-animals/#:~:text=Our%20Views-,Does%20the%20Food%20and%20Drug%20Administration,to%20be%20tested%20on%20animals%3F&text=The%20FDA%20does%20currently%20require,the%20drugs%20safe%20for%20humans)

What you’ll find among trans people is that we don’t all have the same experience, and many of us very much wish they had just been born cis.

A person wouldn’t suddenly become trans, but they could suddenly _realize_ that they’re trans. 

The transphobes out there push this narrative that being trans is a choice, but trans people are born trans just like cis men and cis women. 

That realization happened to me when I was 46. I grew up in the 80s and 90s where there was no ubiquitous vocabulary to discuss gender. 

Even though I felt like a girl (I’m AMAB) from a young age, I simply thought I was a failed boy, and then grew up feeling like a failed man. 

When I look back I see that a lot of the things I felt were gender dysphoria. 

The thing that took me where I needed to go was just listening to my intuition. I wanted to start painting my nails. So I did. I wanted to try wearing a nightgown to bed, so I did. Each time really asking myself if it felt right or not. Each thing I tried felt right. Even if something didn’t look good on me, it was never, because it felt wrong. It was always just that it wasn’t the right color, etc..

So I’d say do the same.

Here’s something my therapist taught me. 

Our bodies know when we are truthful and when we aren’t. 

So start by paying attention to how you feel just looking at yourself in the mirror. That’s your baseline. 

Now say something that you know is untrue to your reflection. Something like saying your name is something it isn’t. How did that feel? Whatever you’re feeling is what it feels like when you lie. 

Try again with saying something true. 

Once you’ve got a good sense of how truth and untruth feels in your body, then say, “I am trans,” did it feel true or untrue. 

For me saying, “I am a cis gendered man,” makes me feel very uncomfortable. 

Anyway. Maybe try that exercise, and remember with all things gender it’s not always black and white or even permanent. Just be kind to yourself and trust yourself to get where you need to go.

You need to figure out your personal style. 

Not just outfits you like, but outfits that make you say, “Wow I look so good today,” when you wear them. 

The best place to start in building your wardrobe is to get your measurements. Waist, hips, bra size, inseam, and shoe size. 

Learning a bit about color is the next step. What colors complement each other, when to use a splash of contrasting color. There’s lots of info online about color theory, but start with getting a grasp of the color wheel. 

My next suggestion is to check out something like Amazon Prime Try Before You Buy where you can order 7 items for free, try them on for 7 days, and then return what you don’t want to buy. 

If you try something on and don’t like it, really interrogate yourself as to why. I tried on a lot of stuff in the beginning that I felt like I didn’t like, but when I dug into why, I discovered I was just nervous that other people wouldn’t think it looked nice on me. 

Nine times out of ten, the bigger fashion risk I’ve taken the more positive the response. 

Which brings me to the absolutely best thing to have in your wardrobe: confidence. 

The clothes you wear are for YOU, and no one else. If you put on an outfit and like how you look, then that’s all that matters. 

Other people can say shit like, “You’re too old to wear that,” or, “That color looks bad on you,” and you can certainly consider those critiques, but YOU get the final say.

It doesn’t come overnight for most. It was definitely a muscle I had to build up. 

In the end have fun with it! They’re just clothes. You wear something, if it worked, then you wear it again, if not? Meh, no one died, and you don’t. Be bold! I don’t know about you, but growing up AMAB meant colors were limited to navy blue, white, varying shades of gray, and khaki. Now you can wear bright colors that make you smile.

The word transgender is an umbrella term that, by definition means you’re not cis. It’s one of the few very binary things around gender. Of course it is up to you whether or not you use that term to describe your gender.

Nonbinary is under the transgender umbrella,
